title: What Was a "Cargo Cult"?
description: A colonial label, the scholars who used it and doubted it, and the 1919 movement that came first

concepts.title: A Label Born in 1945
concepts.contentHtml:
The phrase cargo cult first appeared in print in November 1945, in Pacific Islands Monthly, a magazine read by planters, traders and officials in Australia's Pacific territories. Its writer, Norris Mervyn Bird, called himself an old Territories resident. He worried that wartime upheaval, a softer postwar colonial policy and half-digested Christian teaching would unsettle villagers, and he offered "cargo cult" as a new name for an older label, "Vailala Madness." In Tok Pisin, the pidgin of New Guinea, kago meant goods shipped in from outside, such as tinned food, cloth, steel tools and rifles.

Anthropologists didn't coin the term, but within a few years some of them, including Lucy Mair and Ian Hogbin, had taken it up.1 It soon covered almost any village movement in Melanesia that joined religious hopes to political aims, and a 1979 survey counted 185 of them.2 The textbook pattern went like this. A prophet announces that the ancestors, or a returning hero, will deliver European goods and end white rule, and followers prepare with new rituals, sometimes destroying old ones.

Two classic books set the terms of debate. Peter Worsley's The Trumpet Shall Sound (1957), written from a Marxist standpoint, read the movements as early nationalism, with people split into many small groups finding a shared cause against colonial rule. Peter Lawrence's Road Belong Cargo (1964), on the Madang district of New Guinea and the leader Yali, stressed local reasoning instead. Villagers never saw Europeans making the goods that arrived by ship, so they concluded that wealth came through ritual knowledge, which whites were keeping to themselves.

concepts.title: Why Scholars Now Question the Term
concepts.contentHtml:
By the 1970s, as Melanesian colonies moved toward independence, many anthropologists grew uneasy with "cargo cult," and most have since dropped it. Both words mislead. "Cult" suggests something irrational or fringe. "Cargo" shrinks a wide set of hopes, for respect, moral equality and restored relations with the dead and with Europeans, into a craving for consumer goods. Nancy McDowell argued in 1988 that the label lumps together movements that may have little in common. Martha Kaplan's study of Fiji's Tuka movement, Neither Cargo nor Cult (1995), showed how colonial officials' categories and fears shaped what they recorded and how they policed it.

The anthropologist Lamont Lindstrom, who has done fieldwork on Tanna in Vanuatu for decades, took the term itself as his subject. His book Cargo Cult: Strange Stories of Desire from Melanesia and Beyond (1993) traced how the term traveled from colonial journalism into anthropology and then into Western popular culture. On his reading, cargo cult stories say as much about the West's own restless desire for goods as about Melanesians.

The picture most people carry comes from the physicist Richard Feynman's 1974 Caltech commencement speech, "Cargo Cult Science."1 Islanders build runways, light fires beside them and carve wooden headphones, then wait for planes that never land. Some imitation of this kind was recorded, and on Tanna in 1943 a leader and his followers were arrested while clearing an airfield. But the picture of whole societies frozen in hopeful mimicry is a stereotype. Melanesians now use "cargo cult" as an insult for a rival's foolish scheme. A few scholars, such as Holger Jebens and Ton Otto, defend keeping the term if it is used carefully to name a real pattern.

concepts.title: The Vailala Madness, 1919
concepts.contentHtml:
The movement usually counted as the first well-documented "cargo cult" began in late 1919 in the Gulf Division of Papua, then a territory governed by Australia, among the Elema peoples near the Vailala River. Europeans called it the Vailala Madness because of what struck them first. Men and women were seized by trembling and dizziness, staggering, and speaking in what observers took for tongues.

Its leaders announced that a "ghost steamer" piloted by the returning dead would soon arrive, bringing departed relatives along with goods such as tinned food and tools. Some said rifles too, to drive out the Europeans. Many held that the ancestors would come back white. Followers raised flagpoles that one European took for imitation wireless masts, set tables decorated with croton leaves and ate at them sitting on stools, drilled like soldiers and kept curfews like those of plantation life. Leaders had probably seen such routines while working on distant plantations. Followers also turned on the old religion. The hevehe ceremonial cycle, which could take more than a decade to complete, was abandoned in many villages, and sacred objects once forbidden to women were shown to the uninitiated and destroyed.

The administration jailed several leaders under laws against spreading false reports. The government anthropologist F. E. Williams arrived in 1922, when the movement was still strong but breaking up, and published The Vailala Madness and the Destruction of Native Ceremonies in the Gulf Division (1923). Williams regretted the loss of the old ceremonies and saw the movement as harmful. The steamer never came, and by the late 1920s the movement was no longer active. In 1934 Williams revisited it in "The Vailala Madness in Retrospect."

title: John Frum of Tanna
description: A prophet-figure, an American army, a February holiday and the politics of custom

concepts.title: Tanna Law and the First Sightings
concepts.contentHtml:
Tanna is a volcanic island in the south of what is now Vanuatu. From 1906 the archipelago, then the New Hebrides, was ruled jointly by Britain and France as the Anglo-French Condominium. Presbyterian missionaries had struggled on Tanna in the nineteenth century, but by the 1930s most islanders had joined mission churches. Missionaries and their Tannese helpers enforced rules that islanders came to call Tanna Law, which restricted kava drinking, dancing and other customary practices, among converts and non-converts alike.

Against this background a figure called John Frum began to appear. Accounts on Tanna place his first appearances in the late 1930s, often after elders had drunk kava. The first government record dates from November 1940, when the British District Agent, James Nicol, investigated goats stolen to feed crowds gathering and dancing for John Frum at Green Point. The message, as officials and later followers reported it, told people to give up money, mission schools, churches and plantation work and return to kastom, customary ways, including kava and dancing. The Europeans would leave, and their goods would pass to the Tannese.

In 1941 followers spent their money in a rush at the stores, and on 11 May few Presbyterian converts came to Sunday services. Police arrested suspected leaders in June, among them a man called Manehevi, whom some accounts identify as the man behind the name. He and others were exiled from Tanna. Many Tannese say instead that John Frum was a spirit, linked by some to Keraperamun, a god of Mount Tukosmera.1 Even the name is uncertain. A 1949 administrator derived "Frum" from a local pronunciation of "broom"; others hear "John from America." Neither origin is established.

concepts.title: America Arrives
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1942 United States forces arrived in the New Hebrides and built large bases on Efate and Espiritu Santo. Many Tannese men, John Frum supporters among them, went to work in the American labor corps. As they later remembered it, they met an army with enormous supplies that it shared freely, officers who treated them with more respect than the British and French did, and Black soldiers who wore the same uniforms and handled the same goods as white ones. In Tannese memory America became a land of plenty and fairness, and John Frum came to be linked with it.

The Condominium kept arresting, jailing and exiling leaders from 1941 to 1956. In October 1943 the New Hebrides Defence Force, with American officers, arrested a leader named Neloiag and dozens of followers who were clearing an airfield. By 1956 the authorities stopped treating the movement as subversive. In January 1957 two leaders, Nakomaha and Thomas Nampas, came home to Sulphur Bay on Tanna's east coast, and on 15 February 1957 they raised flags in John Frum's honor: by one account, red warning flags salvaged from wartime fuel dumps. The date became the movement's holiday, now marked with real American flags.

Nakomaha also founded the Tanna Army, a nonviolent ritual company whose members drill with bamboo rifles. When David Attenborough filmed on Tanna in 1959, a follower told him that if people could wait two thousand years for Jesus Christ, he could wait more than nineteen years for John. The remark shows how followers saw their faith, as a promise on its own timetable, comparable to the Christian hope the missions had taught.

concepts.title: John Frum Day and the Politics of Kastom
concepts.contentHtml:
Each 15 February, followers gather at Lamakara, a village above Sulphur Bay, near the smoking cone of Mount Yasur, the volcano where many believe John Frum lives. Men dressed in imitation American uniforms march with bamboo rifles whose sharpened tips are painted red, some with "USA" painted in red on their chests and backs. Flags are raised, and there are speeches, dances and kava. Chief Isaac Wan, the movement's leader at Lamakara for decades, told visitors that he spoke regularly with John Frum, and called him "our God, our Jesus." Friday-night dances draw followers and, increasingly, tourists.

The movement has always been political as well. In the 1970s supporters backed the French-supported "Moderate" parties against the party that led the New Hebrides to independence. When independent Vanuatu was born in 1980, John Frum followers joined efforts to detach Tanna, which government forces suppressed. Since then the movement has fielded candidates in national elections, and in 1998 one won a seat in parliament.1 In 2000 it split, when a prophet named Fred Nase founded a breakaway Unity movement, leaving three rival centers.

Lindstrom and other scholars read John Frum as kastom politics. By claiming a powerful foreign friend, Tannese could stand apart from the British, the French and the Presbyterian church, and defend kava, dancing and the right to run their own affairs. "America" served as a symbol of an alternative to the colonial order. For members it is also a living religion, and they see no need to choose between faith and politics. Its numbers have fallen since the late twentieth century, but the movement is still active.

title: The Prince Philip Movement
description: How a Tanna legend came to center on the Duke of Edinburgh, and what happened when he died

concepts.title: A Spirit's Son Overseas
concepts.contentHtml:
Elsewhere on Tanna, the people of Yaohnanen and Yakel on Tanna came to revere a different outsider: Prince Philip, Duke of Edinburgh (1921 to 2021). These are kastom communities, which have chosen to keep customary dress, ritual and law and to stay apart from the churches. Their belief built on an old local story. A son of a mountain spirit had traveled to a distant land, married a powerful woman, and would one day return. In some tellings he was a brother of John Frum.

When the son became identified with Philip is unclear; most accounts suggest the 1950s or 1960s. Villagers saw colonial officials treat Queen Elizabeth II, and even her portrait, with great respect. Her husband, they reasoned, must be a man of power from elsewhere, and so the son of the legend, with Britain as the distant land. The anthropologist Kirk Huffman, who has worked in Vanuatu for decades, summed up the belief: Philip "left the island, in his original spiritual form, to find a powerful wife overseas."1

In 1974 the Queen and Philip toured the New Hebrides aboard the royal yacht Britannia. Reports disagree on whether the royal party set foot on Tanna. Some villagers saw Philip, at least from a distance, and Chief Jack Naiva later said he had paddled one of the war canoes that greeted Britannia at Port Vila. For believers, seeing him confirmed what they already held. Philip himself knew nothing of it until several years later, when John Champion, the British Resident Commissioner in the New Hebrides, told him about the villages that honored him.

concepts.title: Photographs and a Pig-Killing Club
concepts.contentHtml:
Champion suggested that the Duke send a portrait, and Philip mailed a signed official photograph. The villagers replied with a gift of their own, a nal-nal, a traditional club for killing pigs. Philip then had himself photographed holding the club and sent that picture too. A third photograph followed in 2000. Chief Jack Naiva kept all three until his death in 2009, and the pictures, with letters from the Palace, became treasured objects. Press reports describe villagers asking Philip's blessing on their gardens.

In 2007 the British broadcaster Channel 4 brought five Tanna men to Britain for a series called Meet the Natives, broadcast that September. Their trip ended with a private, off-camera meeting with the Duke, at which they exchanged gifts and received a new photograph.1 Other royals kept up the link. Princess Anne visited Tanna in 2014, and in 2018 Prince Charles, visiting Vanuatu, was given the chiefly title Mal Menaringmanu at Port Vila.

Despite the press label, the movement involves little expectation of goods. Huffman described the belief as concerned with peace and respect for tradition. As he told it, villagers held that Philip was working to bring those things to Britain and the wider world and could return once he succeeded, but that "white people's stupidity, jealousy, greed and perpetual fighting" stood in the way. The link resembles John Frum's America: a distant, powerful ally who honors kastom, giving a small community standing in a world shaped by outsiders.

concepts.title: After the Duke's Death in 2021
concepts.contentHtml:
Prince Philip died at Windsor on 9 April 2021, aged 99. When the news reached Tanna, the villages went into mourning. The Union flag flew at half-mast on the nakamal, the open ground where men gather to drink kava. Chiefs met at Yaohnanen to discuss what the death meant and sent a message of condolence to the royal family. Mourners planned ritual wailing, songs and dancing, and a communal feast with slaughtered pigs, kava and laplap, the pudding of grated root crops baked in leaves that serves as Vanuatu's national dish.

The death posed a real theological question: where would the Duke's spirit go? A Yakel chief named Albi told the AFP news agency, "The spirit of Prince Philip has left his body, but it lives on; it is too soon to say where it will reside." Others in the villages said his spirit was still with them. Huffman predicted that devotion would pass to Charles, now King Charles III. Some elders argued that Charles was already the rightful successor, because he had received a chiefly title in 2018, while others said nothing was settled. A tribal leader, Chief Yapa, told Reuters that the bond between the people of Tanna and the English remained very strong.

Movements centered on a living person face their sharpest test when that person dies. The Yaohnanen response followed a pattern seen in other religions: the relationship was reinterpreted rather than abandoned, and the spirit became the focus. Press accounts in 2021 put the number of followers at a few hundred, smaller than in earlier decades.

title: The Ghost Dance
description: A Paiute prophet's vision of peace, its spread across the West, and the massacre at Wounded Knee

concepts.title: Wovoka's Vision
concepts.contentHtml:
The Ghost Dance began among the Northern Paiute of western Nevada. Its prophet, Wovoka, was born around 1856 and for many years worked on the ranch of David Wilson near Yerington, where he was known as Jack Wilson and learned Bible stories from the devout Wilson family. He was not the first Paiute prophet of this kind. Around 1869 a healer named Wodziwob had led dances announcing that the dead would soon return, after a typhoid epidemic killed about a tenth of the Northern Paiute.

Wovoka said that during the solar eclipse of 1 January 1889, while gravely ill, he was taken to the other world,1 where he saw God and the dead living happily, and was given a dance and a message. Accounts differ on details, and one scholar dates his first vision to 1887. His teaching survives best in the "Messiah Letter," dictated to Cheyenne and Arapaho visitors in August 1891 and published by the Smithsonian ethnologist James Mooney, who interviewed Wovoka in January 1892. "You must not fight," it says. "Do right always." It also told followers not to refuse to work for whites. People were to dance for four nights, and on the last night until the morning of the fifth day; then the dead would be reunited with the living and the earth renewed.

The dance itself was a circle dance with joined hands, built on the Paiute round dance. His own message joined Christian ideas, such as a coming renewal and the ethic of nonviolence, to Paiute traditions of prophecy. Once it left Nevada, though, other nations read it through their own histories and hopes.

concepts.title: Across the Plains: Ghost Shirts
concepts.contentHtml:
News of the prophet spread in 1889 and 1890 by railroad journeys, word of mouth and letters written by young people schooled in English. Delegations came from many nations, and the dance was taken up by the Shoshone, Arapaho, Cheyenne, Kiowa, Caddo, Pawnee, Lakota and others. Each reshaped it with its own songs, visions and leaders. Not everyone was persuaded: the Navajo, among others, largely declined it.

The Lakota came to the dance in desperate times. The bison herds that had sustained Plains life were gone by the mid-1880s. A land agreement of 1889 broke up the Great Sioux Reservation into smaller reservations and opened millions of acres to settlers. In 1890 crops failed, epidemics struck, and the government cut rations. Lakota delegates, among them Short Bull and Kicking Bear, traveled to Nevada in late 1889 and returned in the spring of 1890 with the new teaching. Some Lakota teachers said a new earth would cover the old, sweeping away the whites, while believers would be restored to a world full of bison and their dead kin.

Lakota dancers wore ghost shirts: muslin or buckskin garments painted with stars, moons, birds and other sacred images. Many believed the shirts had protective power, and some said they would stop bullets.1 Their origin is uncertain. Kicking Bear is said to have introduced them to the Lakota, and Mooney guessed at a link to the sacred undergarment worn by Latter-day Saints, an idea that remains unproven. The shirts do not appear in the Messiah Letter as Mooney recorded it.

concepts.title: Wounded Knee and a Misread Revival
concepts.contentHtml:
Agents, settlers and newspapers saw the dancing as a prelude to war; the press called it the "Messiah craze." In November 1890 Daniel Royer, the inexperienced new agent at Pine Ridge, called for troops, and thousands of soldiers moved onto the Lakota reservations. Some dancers withdrew with Short Bull and Kicking Bear to the Stronghold, a natural fortress in the Badlands. On 15 December 1890 Indian police sent to arrest Sitting Bull at Standing Rock, shot him dead in a fight at his home.

Spotted Elk, also called Big Foot, a Miniconjou leader ill with pneumonia, set out for Pine Ridge with about 350 people. The 7th Cavalry intercepted the band and camped it at Wounded Knee Creek. On 29 December 1890, under Colonel James Forsyth, soldiers began disarming the Lakota. A rifle went off in a struggle, and the troops opened fire, including Hotchkiss guns. Estimates of Lakota dead range from about 250 to 300, many of them women and children. Twenty-five soldiers died, some probably from their own side's crossfire. About twenty soldiers later received the Medal of Honor.1 In 1990 Congress passed a resolution expressing "deep regret" for the massacre.

Most historians, among them Jeffrey Ostler (2004), conclude that the Lakota Ghost Dancers planned no armed uprising. They hoped for a world made new by divine action, not by Lakota rifles, and the authorities misread a religious revival as a military threat. Louis Warren (2017) adds that Wovoka's religion of peace and work helped followers adapt to reservation life. The dance outlived 1890: it continued among several nations, the Caddo still practice it, and Lakota participants performed it during the 1973 occupation of Wounded Knee.

title: The Xhosa Cattle-Killing
description: Nongqawuse's prophecy of 1856, the famine that followed, and the argument over the governor's role

concepts.title: A Frontier Under Strain
concepts.contentHtml:
By the 1850s the Xhosa, cattle-keeping farmers on the eastern frontier of the British Cape Colony, had fought the colony in a long series of frontier wars stretching back to 1779. The eighth and most bitter, the War of Mlanjeni (1850 to 1853), took its name from a young prophet who had promised his followers protection against the colonists' bullets. The Xhosa lost. West of the Kei River, chiefdoms such as Sandile's Ngqika lived under British rule in the territory of British Kaffraria. East of the Kei, the Gcaleka under the paramount chief Sarhili stayed independent.

Cattle were the center of Xhosa life: wealth, food, the payment that sealed a marriage, and the animals sacrificed to the ancestors. In 1853 a cattle disease, bovine pleuropneumonia or "lungsickness," reached the Cape with imported European cattle. By 1854 it was spreading through Xhosa herds and killing animals in huge numbers. Many Xhosa saw the epidemic as a sign of deeper disorder, often blamed on witchcraft.

The new governor, Sir George Grey, arrived at the Cape at the end of 1854 after governing South Australia and New Zealand. He set out to "civilize" the Xhosa: magistrates to oversee chiefs, salaries to replace chiefs' traditional fines and fees, public works using Xhosa labor, and plans to settle Europeans among them. To many Xhosa, this program meant the slow loss of land, power and independence. Earlier prophets had answered such pressures before. Around 1818 the prophet Nxele preached that the dead would rise and the whites be driven out, and in 1819 he led an attack on colonial Grahamstown.

concepts.title: Nongqawuse's Prophecy
concepts.contentHtml:
In April 1856 Nongqawuse, an orphan of about fifteen, went with a younger girl, Nombanda, to scare birds from the crops near the mouth of the Gxarha River, in Sarhili's country. She came back saying she had met two strangers who said they were ancestors long dead. She told her uncle and guardian, Mhlakaza, a diviner who had lived in the Cape Colony and knew Christian teaching. The historian Jeff Peires has argued that he was the man known in mission records as Wilhelm Goliath, a Xhosa convert who had served the Anglican archdeacon Nathaniel Merriman.

The message grew as the months passed. The Xhosa were to kill their cattle, destroy their stored grain, and stop planting. They were to give up witchcraft and adultery. In return the dead would rise, new and healthy cattle would fill the kraals, grain pits would overflow, and the settlers would be swept into the sea.1 The prophecy joined Xhosa ideas about the ancestors to the Christian idea of resurrection. Sarhili accepted it, and the killing spread across Xhosaland and into British Kaffraria. Another young prophet, Nonkosi, also had visions.

The Xhosa split. A minority called the amagogotya refused to kill their cattle, and believers blamed them for each delay. The day of fulfillment moved several times. The great day was finally set for 18 February 1857, when the sun was to rise blood-red. It rose as usual. Sarhili named another date eight days later, which also passed. The movement collapsed over the following months, by which time most of the cattle were dead and the grain was gone.

concepts.title: Famine and the Argument over Grey
concepts.contentHtml:
Peires estimates that about 400,000 cattle were killed and about 40,000 Xhosa died of starvation,1 while tens of thousands more left home in search of food and work. Precise figures are impossible; these are reconstructions from colonial records. The population of British Kaffraria fell from about 105,000 to fewer than 27,000, a drop that counts migration as well as death.

Grey's response has been argued over ever since. Relief was offered mainly to those who entered labor contracts with colonial employers, and thousands of starving Xhosa were sent into the Cape Colony as workers. Grey confiscated large areas of Xhosa land and opened them to white settlers, including German military settlers. He promoted a "Chiefs' Plot" theory, which held that the cattle-killing was a scheme by chiefs to drive desperate warriors against the colony, and he used it to arrest chiefs. Some, including the veteran war leader Maqoma, were imprisoned on Robben Island.

A belief found in Xhosa popular memory goes further: that Grey or colonial agents staged the strangers' appearance to Nongqawuse. Historians, Peires among them, have found no evidence for this. Peires's own position, in The Dead Will Arise (1989), is that the movement was a Xhosa response to real crisis, which Grey did not cause but deliberately exploited to break Xhosa independence. Helen Bradford has argued that such accounts still neglect gender, including what it meant that the prophets were girls. Nongqawuse herself was handed to the British, held for a time in Cape Town, and later lived on a farm in the Alexandria district, where she died in 1898. The South African novelist Zakes Mda retold her story in The Heart of Redness (2000).

title: Hong Xiuquan and the Prophets of Crisis
description: A failed scholar's visions, the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom, and what these movements share

concepts.title: Hong Xiuquan's Visions
concepts.contentHtml:
Hong Xiuquan was born in 1814 into a Hakka farming family in Hua county, near Guangzhou. The Hakka, a Chinese group with their own dialect and customs, were often at odds with their neighbors. The family scraped together money for his schooling in the hope that he would pass the civil service examinations, the path to office and status in Qing China. He failed the qualifying examination at Guangzhou four times, in 1836, 1837 and 1843 among them.

In Guangzhou around 1836 he was handed a set of Christian tracts, Good Words to Admonish the Age, by Liang Fa, a Chinese convert who worked with Protestant missionaries. He barely read them. After his failure in 1837 he fell seriously ill and had visions. In the later Taiping account, he was carried to heaven, where an old man with a golden beard gave him a sword and a seal and ordered him to slay demons, helped by an elder brother. Confucius, in one version, was rebuked for misleading the Chinese.

After his last failure in 1843, Hong read Liang Fa's tracts properly and found in them an explanation of his visions. The old man was God the Father; the elder brother was Jesus; and Hong himself was God's second son, sent to rid China of demons, by which he came to mean idols and in time the Manchu rulers. He began destroying idols. His friend Feng Yunshan founded a God Worshippers society among poor Hakka in the hills of Guangxi. In 1847 Hong studied for some months in Guangzhou with the American Southern Baptist missionary Issachar Roberts, who declined to baptize him.

concepts.title: The Heavenly Kingdom, 1851 to 1864
concepts.contentHtml:
Defeat by Britain in the First Opium War ended with the Treaty of Nanjing in 1842, and southern China was racked by banditry, famine and Hakka feuds. In Guangxi the God Worshippers armed themselves. In January 1851, at Jintian, Hong proclaimed the Taiping Tianguo, the Heavenly Kingdom of Great Peace.1 The Taiping armies marched north and in March 1853 took Nanjing, which they renamed Tianjing, the Heavenly Capital, and held for eleven years.

The kingdom tried to remake society. It separated men and women, banned opium, alcohol and foot binding, held its own examinations on its own scriptures, and published a plan to share land equally that was never carried out. Yang Xiuqing claimed that God the Father spoke through him, and Xiao Chaogui spoke as Jesus, voices that could overrule Hong himself. In 1856 Hong had Yang killed, and thousands of Yang's followers died in the purge. From 1859 Hong's cousin Hong Rengan proposed modernizing reforms, to little effect.

Western powers mostly backed the Qing. The Ever Victorious Army, Chinese troops under Western officers led by Frederick Townsend Ward and then Charles Gordon, fought near Shanghai, while Zeng Guofan's Xiang Army from Hunan bore the main burden of the war. Hong died on 1 June 1864, during the siege of Nanjing, probably of illness, though suicide has also been suggested; the city fell in July, and the last Taiping army was destroyed in 1871. Most historians estimate 20 to 30 million deaths, chiefly from famine and disease alongside battle and massacre; some estimates run much higher, and all rest on incomplete records. Stephen Platt and others prefer to call it a civil war.

concepts.title: Prophets of Crisis Compared
concepts.contentHtml:
Scholars have long compared these movements. In 1956 the anthropologist Anthony F. C. Wallace described "revitalization movements": deliberate efforts to build a more satisfying culture, usually launched by a prophet's vision at a time of severe stress. His model case was the Seneca prophet Handsome Lake, whose visions began in 1799. Peter Worsley (1957), Vittorio Lanternari's The Religions of the Oppressed (Italian 1960, English 1963) and Michael Adas's Prophets of Rebellion (1979) compared prophet-led movements against colonial rule across several continents.

The cases in this topic share real features. Each arose under colonial or imperial pressure, often after epidemics or ecological losses: lungsickness among Xhosa cattle, the end of the bison, defeat in the Opium War. Their prophets were usually marginal figures, such as a teenage orphan girl, a Paiute ranch hand and a failed examination candidate. Most reworked Christian ideas, from Wovoka's ethic of peace and Mhlakaza's resurrection to Hong's heavenly family; even John Frum's rejection of the missions borrowed the language of a Second Coming. Several promised the return of the dead and a renewed world.

The outcomes could hardly differ more. The Ghost Dance taught peace and was met with massacre; the cattle-killing destroyed its own believers' livelihood; the Taiping built a state and fought one of history's deadliest wars; John Frum became a lasting local politics. Scholars also warn against reading every movement only as a response to crisis. That reading can reduce faith to a symptom and ignore older roots, such as Paiute prophecy before Wovoka, Xhosa prophets before Nongqawuse and Melanesian myths of returning ancestors. Many of the labels, from "madness" to "cult" and "craze," came from officials.
